items.description: maxxing the ability to run different LLMs on the smallest devices possible

readme.excerpt:
Run the biggest language model you can on the smallest hardware you own.

TV boxes, old phones and tablets, single-board computers and routers all have a CPU, some RAM and flash storage that sit idle most of the day. smolmaxxing finds the biggest model each of them can really run, then pushes it further with custom kernels, careful memory use and weights streamed from flash. Every number in this repo was measured on the device itself.

items.name: moraine
items.description: Run DuckLake entirely in object storage, no server required. A SlateDB-backed catalog, as a DuckDB extension and a Rust crate.

readme.excerpt:
Run DuckLake entirely in object storage, no server required. Documentation: .

DuckLake stores table data as Parquet files in object storage and hosts its catalog in a SQL database: SQLite, Postgres, or DuckDB (served over Quack). The database layer provides transactional consistency and ACID guarantees, but requires hosting an additional server.

Moraine removes the need for a separate catalog database. Instead, it serves the catalog from SlateDB, an embedded transactional key-value store that also lives in object storage. That means that the catalog resides in the same bucket as the data files. In addition, Moraine is the only DuckLake extension that offers DuckDB native indexes for faster querying.

items.name: unkernel
items.description: A real Linux kernel, compiled to WebAssembly. It boots to a shell in less than a second.

readme.excerpt:
A real Linux kernel, compiled to WebAssembly. It boots to a shell in less than a second.

Try it · Performance · Features · CLI · How it works · Benchmarks · JavaScript SDK

unkernel is Linux 7.x built as a single wasm module with a real MMU. The kernel (syscalls, scheduler, memory management, ext4, TCP/IP) is compiled code, not emulated, so programs get Linux's own behavior down to the edge cases. Only user programs are emulated: unmodified aarch64 (arm64) Linux binaries, so Alpine and Debian packages run as they are.

ImageMagick® is a free and open-source software suite, used for editing and manipulating digital images. It can be used to create, edit, compose, or convert bitmap images, and supports a wide range of file formats, including JPEG, PNG, GIF, TIFF, and PDF.

ImageMagick is widely used in industries such as web development, graphic design, and video editing, as well as in scientific research, medical imaging, and astronomy. Its versatile and customizable nature, along with its robust image processing capabilities, make it a popular choice for a wide range of image-related tasks.

ImageMagick includes a command-line interface for executing complex image processing tasks, as well as APIs for integrating its features into software applications. It is written in C and can be used on a variety of operating systems, including Linux, Windows, and macOS.

items.name: zephyr
items.description: Primary Git Repository for the Zephyr Project. Zephyr is a new generation, scalable, optimized, secure RTOS for multiple hardware architectures.

readme.excerpt:
The Zephyr Project is a scalable real-time operating system (RTOS) supporting multiple hardware architectures, optimized for resource constrained devices, and built with security in mind.

The Zephyr OS is based on a small-footprint kernel designed for use on resource-constrained systems: from simple embedded environmental sensors and LED wearables to sophisticated smart watches and IoT wireless gateways.

The Zephyr kernel supports multiple architectures, including ARM (Cortex-A, Cortex-R, Cortex-M), Intel x86, ARC, Tensilica Xtensa, and RISC-V, SPARC, MIPS, and a large number of supported boards .

items.name: xcl
items.description: Xbox Series compatibility layer for Windows - runs console game code natively, reimplements the console system libraries and recompiles RDNA2 shaders to DXIL

readme.excerpt:
XCL runs Xbox Series X S (GDK) game files on a Windows PC without CPU emulation : the game's x64 code runs natively and XCL stands in for the console libraries the PC does not have ( kernelx.dll , XGameRuntime, d3d12 xs.dll , …) – in the spirit of Wine/Proton. The console's GPU code (RDNA2 machine code) is recompiled into PC shaders (HLSL → DXIL).

Project state: retail games run – Minecraft Preview and Unicorn Overlord are fully playable, Fortnite and XDefiant work as far as each game goes without its online services; see Games. The foundation is tested against real data from retail games (shader packs, texture archives, movies and the console DLLs they ship). Details, measurements and next steps: HANDOFF.md ; design: docs/specs/2026-11-20-xcl-design.md .

- 100 % of a retail game's shaders translate – all 26 698 RDNA2 programs (26 503 records) of its shader pack become HLSL; random samples compile to DXIL with 0 errors. - The game's own console DLLs run on the PC – its Bink 2 video codec decodes the game's movies, its ray-tracing BVH builder builds acceleration structures on a PC GPU, the AMD FSR 4 console upscaler runs a whole frame on a PC GPU, the GDK HTTP library initialises. - Console textures decode exactly – the GFX10 tiling and mip layout reproduce 909 of 912 textures of the game's texture archive byte for byte, its volume textures included. - 370+ automated tests , including GPU tests that compare translated shaders against expected results instruction by instructi
